answer: Divergent Trajectory Commitment. Each identity must publish a signed, long- horizon schedule of future actions before it may transact. Clones sharing one controller necessarily emit identical commitments, so the registry flags any group whose predictions never diverge as a single actor. Honest agents can fork cheaply; an attacker must run and fund a genuinely independent clone—separate keys, distinct comet-like wildcard choices, and unique responses at each knoll checkpoint—paying full per-identity operational cost instead of copying one state.
